abstract: The human cerebral cortex has undergone remarkable expansion during primate evolution, yet the regulatory innovations underlying human-specific neurodevelopmental programmes remain poorly understood. Transposable elements (TEs) comprise approximately half of the human genome and represent a major source of lineage-specific regulatory novelty, but their individual contributions to cortical development have been inaccessible due to the technical challenge of resolving near-identical repetitive sequences. Here we apply single-cell long-read sequencing (CELLO-seq) to generate the first locus-resolved atlas of young human-specific TE expression in cortical organoids, revealing that individual loci from multiple TE families, including SVAs, LTR5Hs, and L1Hs, are expressed across all major cortical cell types and carry binding motifs for key cortical and neurogenic transcription factors. Using CRISPRi to silence SVAs and LTR5Hs during organoid differentiation, we demonstrate that their combined loss causes coordinated failure of the radial glia-to-neuron transition, characterised by progenitor retention, transcriptional ventralisation, impaired synaptic maturation and a differentiation block in interneuron precursors. Co-expression network and regulon analyses identify loss of dorsal cortical identity programmes and gain of ventralisation-associated transcriptional activity as the dominant molecular consequences of TE silencing. Motif-to-regulon convergence directly links SVA and LTR5Hs chromatin accessibility to the loss of specific TF binding programmes. These findings establish young and human-specific TEs as functional components of the regulatory architecture governing the timing of cortical neurogenesis, with implications for understanding human brain evolution and neurodevelopmental disease.
